p: Yeah, yeah.

So, as a Jewish New Yorker I experience antisemitism in ways that are somewhat different than more visibly Jewish New Yorkers who obviously experience the lionshare of person-to-person antisemitism, but of course, walking through the subway– I’ll give you an example. Yesterday, there was something at 42nd Street at NQR line that said death to all Jews. so, as a Jewish person, of course, I experience that as threatening and scary and troubling. And in my capacity, I have someone I can email when I see that and try to get it taken care of. But yes.

Okay. Okay. I don’t– you know, it’s not something that I like to claim, but it’s clear, I don’t– I think as one of you mentioned earlier, it’s obviously clear that the reason the rise in Brooklyn is so significant is that the– is that in Brooklyn particularly people look like me. It’s not hard. You know, other than the old unfortunate joke about somebody thinking that I’m Amish and not Jewish. But that’s the fact. That’s the fact. And particularly, women are– you know, if they’re walking around do not, you know, clearly– even Orthodox Jewish women many are– it’s not clear.

The last thing I want to mention is that there is a new trend, and this has been going on recently, and I think it’s very, very unhelpful and contributes to the increase in hate. Many elected officials throughout the city when they talk about hate against Jews, the next thing they say is Islamophobia, although there’s no competition, again, about hate. This is not something. But the numbers don’t make sense. For example, years ago if somebody had said that hate against Jews and Islamophobia, the gay community rightfully would be up in arms, rightfully, to say are you kidding me? The numbers that the Police Department has, there are greater numbers of hate against members of the gay community than issues of Islamophobia, and automatically–
[interposing] Thank you, Council Member.

that is a contribution unfortunately to some who can’t control themselves that contributes. All I would say is that when people talk about it, when elected officials discuss hate, if they– even the Commissioner who’s doing a great job, it’s been a new trend.
Thank you, Council Member.
Yeah. You’re not going to shut me up, but you know, you can– all I’m suggesting–
[interposing] Never.

but I’ll shut– you allowed somebody else to finish their thought. So, all I’m suggesting again it’s not a competition and it’s not towards the Mayor’s person either, but when elected officials talk about hate– if they want to talk about it in order of number, that’s fine. If they want to talk about it in some order, other order, that’s also fine. But putting those two together, especially since October 7th, does not help at all.
Thank you. You can answer.
I actually didn’t hear a question, but I appreciate that feedback. Thank you.

That’s fine. Let’s move on to– back to DA Gonzalez. DA Gonzalez, what

do you think regarding the changes in the way that NYPD is reporting hate crimes?

Well, to– Council Member, I’m actually being informed of the practice today more clearly. I have no issues with the Police Department making sure that their numbers are accurate. I think it makes sense for the public to know accuracy of incidents. You know, it’s also important, and I think Commissioner Gerber said this, that you know there are things that get reported that may not meet the penal law definition of a hate crime, but these bias incidents have to exist somewhere, and as long as the Police Department is also, you know, publishing the number of reported incidents that they’ve looked at, I think that it satisfies us. My only concern as District Attorney is that obviously we’re the people who are given the authority under the law to charge that these incidents also be given to my office so that my attorneys can look at it. Because there have been times where we’ve upgraded the charge where the police did not find a hate crime, but we presented to a grand jury and a grand jury did find a hate crime. And so we want to make sure that we’re part of that

decision making process. But accuracy is a good thing for the City of New York.
Thank you. And if you know, how many hate crimes did you prosecute say in the last five years, and how many of them were antisemitic hate crimes?

I would have to look at the numbers, but of all the incidents that I described and think this sometimes is a shocking thing when I have to, you know, say it out loud. There were 35 arrests last year of all the hate crimes that were committed in Brooklyn that were antisemitic. So, you know, there were 35 arrests and then 10 juvenile arrests which my office no longer sees. I would have to go back and do the math, and I’m happy to report it back to you, Council Member.
That’s fine. If you could provide that information to us, we would appreciate it.
sure.

And I know you touched on this earlier, but what do you think is fueling this disproportionate hate crimes, these

disproportionate hate crimes against the Jewish New Yorkers?

Unfortunately, I think there’s a lot of bias and a lot of hate, and you know, it’s quite honestly I think people are emboldened to act out, and you know, it requires the combination of education, prevention and enforcement, and all three are important, but when we deal with the young people– we saw that terrible incident where I know that the Speaker Julie Menin went into Brooklyn with the swastikas all over the playground. Those are 15-year-old children painting, you know, dozens and dozens of swastikas. And so there has to be more done on the prevention. I’ve seen it as District Attorney on some of these cases. When I confront young people that have been arrested, they don’t understand the history. They’re unaware of the meaning of a lot of these incidents, and quite frankly I think social media fuels a lot of the hate.
You mentioned you believe they’re emboldened to act out. Is there a reason you think that they’re emboldened to act out more now than before?

I think it’s social media. I think that people try to get a reaction, and hearing the coverage of the war and after October 7th, there’s been a lot of information put on social media that is inaccurate and causes people to want to speak out, and sometimes that causes them to act out as well. And we just want to make sure that we hold folks accountable for what they actually do, but we want to make sure that we’re not ignoring young people and making sure that they get accurate information. And I think you heard Council Member Felder say, like the education piece that’s not happening is a critical piece of why I think antisemitic violence is on the increase, because young people actually don’t the know the history.
Okay. Thank you. And you mentioned you have a Hate Crimes Bureau at Brooklyn DA’s office, correct?
I have an unfunded bureau which I’m hoping that the City Council will help–
[interposing] Let’s talk about that.
The City Council will help fund.
What– can you tell us exactly what this bureau does?

Our bureau was created when I first was elected, because I started to see an increase in hate crimes in the country. In most offices– so we had the first dedicated Hate Crimes Bureau in New York City. in most offices, ADAs prosecute hate crimes and they may prosecute other types of cases. I thought we needed people who specialized understanding the evidentiary challenges that we’ve already discussed in these cases, but also because these folks need to be in the community whether it be the LGBTQ community, the Jewish community, whatever community has to– you know, has to feel protected. They need to be in the community doing the work with the community, earning cultural competence and quite honestly, that bureau needs to speak the different languages and represent people so they feel comfortable reporting. And our bureau has been charged with not just prosecuting

cases, but trying to prevent cases. So, we’ve been in schools. We do community functions. We’re out presenting with the Police Department and community organizations, and you know, the fact that every other DA’s office has now been funded to do this, I think the people of Brooklyn deserve to be funded with a dedicated unit, and I’ll add, more resources.
How many staff members does the bureau currently have?
Currently, there are six dedicated prosecutors, and four, you know, analysts and clerks. So, 10 in right now, and we need more.
And can you talk a little more about the funding? How much funding are you currently getting? Who are you getting it from, and how much funding you think you need and requested?

When I testified at the City Council Public Safety Committee, I asked for $1.5 million to create a dedicated Hate Crimes Unit that would be funded like some of the other– like the Manhattan DAs office or the Queens DA office. We should have similar

funding. We receive $50,000 from the City Council to fight all hate crimes, $50,000. And other offices receive, you know, in excess of a million.
And we can just a little bit about what the DA’s office you’ll be doing with that funding within the bureau.

Yeah, so we would be doing a lot of the prevention work, working alongside with our partners in the community. We would be hiring more senior investigators. You know, a lot of this work in a successful prosecution really does take deep dives into who the accused are. We would have analysts and we would have paralegals and clerks, and we would be able to hire more senior prosecutors to do this work. Right now, hate crimes as they’re growing in our city, as we see it was eight percent down this year so far, but that increase has not seen more funding for additional staff to handle the surge in hate.
THank you very much. Those are all my question. DA Gonzalez, thank you again, for–
[interposing] Thank you.
being here today. I’ll pass it over to Chair Dinowitz.

Thank you so much, Chair Vernikov. We’ve heard mention from in various ways youth, a lot about youth. Does the NYPD or the DA’s Office or the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism in any way disaggregate hate crime data based on age?

Yeah, I don’t– we surely don’t have it here, and I don’t think that we track it that way. We obviously track many things with hate crime data, but I don’t think we track it in terms of age of the perpetrator.
Right. Well, I don’t believe it’s published on your hate crimes dashboard.
Definitely not.
Nor in the Open Data.
Yeah.

Is there any reason why we couldn’t disaggregate that data by age range, especially if you’re here testifying saying

that there are differences between youth and education and school youth who are perpetrating hate crimes, and adults, people who are out of school. NYPD, DA’s Office, Mayor’s Office oppose disaggregating that data by age range?

I think we could. I would obviously want to check with our data people to make sure we’re not missing something, but yes. I don’t see why we could not going forward track the data that way. I understand your point. I take the point. And again, I would want to confirm it to make sure we’re not missing something in terms of how data comes in, how we do it, but point is well-taken.

And I would support it completely to do that, because part of the conversations I have as District Attorney is when we’re dealing with the community and crime victims, having to explain to them when a case comes to the DA’s office versus when it’s sent to Family Court. There’s a lot of confusion around who the prosecuting agency is, and so if it’s aggregated by age, the community could understand what percentage of cases actually go to the DA’s Office versus family court or handled in those kinds of adjudications.

Yeah. And as we have all mentioned multiple times, a hate crime feels more of a community– an attack on a community. And so there– I believe communities often feel different about kids than they may about adults. And so that is an important data point in us addressing hate crimes and knowing how to attack it. But I do also want to talk about, you know, that information that’s shared with the communities. Right? Right now, on the hate crimes dashboard they list out type of hate crime whether it’s Jewish, anti-gay, anti-Black, all of that. It indicates whether an arrest was made. What it does not indicate is the disposition of a case once an arrest is made. And that’s, to my knowledge, public information, but it is not publicly available on the dashboard. What steps need to be taken to include that really critical information about what happens to the person after they’re arrested on the dashboard so entire communities can have peace of mind or know what next steps they have to take as a community?

Totally understood about the importance of that piece. No debate there. The slight challenge I guess I would

say is, what you have on the NYPD hate crimes dashboard is NYPD data. That is data that we maintain and we track and all that. When it comes to court dispositions, that’s not our data, right? So, that’s going to be– we look at different ways. Obviously, different prosecutor’s offices will track what they’re doing and then OCA will obviously have their data. I want to be clear, of course, on a one-off basis, you know, detectives should know what’s happening in their cases. I’m not suggesting we don’t know what happens in individual cases. In terms of the rigorous tracking of data, right, those dispositions is not– that’s not NYPD data. That’s going to be court data.
But is the data easy enough to get? You may not own it on your website, but is it publicly available, or is it difficult to get from a DA’s office?
Right. So–

[interposing] I’ll jump in just because sometimes it’s not as gratifying data because cases take so long, right? So, an arrest from 2025, there will be recorded disposition that– at the end of that year, because

the case kicks in to 2026. Sometimes the person is in mental health, but it may last to 2027. So, reported dispositions often run a year, a year and a half after the commission of that crime. What we try to do in our office is publicly report out. There’s dashboards, and I think the– during the public reporting part at the end of the fiscal year– I’m sorry, at the end of the calendar year, every March, the DA’s offices report data including disposition data. So, we could try to– what I can– what I’ll commit to doing is making that data more easily accessible to the City Council. But all that information is available on the computer except for juveniles. And I think when juveniles become really frustrating to our community members– they’re not allowed to know the perpetrator’s names or the outcomes of the adjudications that happened in those cases, and I think that is a real black hole in the reporting structure.

Sure. I mean, that speaks to the importance of disaggregating by age range, but it sounds like we have two agencies here who aren’t opposed to sharing the information. So, you hold the data. You report on other data. But if

the data were, you know, were available in an easily digestible form which it seems like the Brooklyn DA’s already providing but is willing to do the work to provide more. Is the NYPD willing to include it on their dashboard and in their–

[interposing] Certainly open to exploring. Certainly open to exploring it. I do want to emphasize, it is a little more complicated. First of all, when you have– I’m not the data expert. But when you have other entities, different DAs offices, they’re– would not shock me. It is not necessarily tracking the same systems in the same way. Connecting that in, like linking between each of the DA’s offices, right– linking that data and their– may be differences, I don’t even know. In their various systems–
[interposing] Sorry, it seems very complicated. How many hate crimes were there in 2025?
Okay 556?
166 confirmed hate crimes.
I can’t hear you. I’m sorry.
In 2025, there were 566 confirmed–
Yeah.

You know, we’re not talking about large data sets here. 566– we’re talking about only five District Attorney’s offices. I mean, you may be talking about a little manual labor, but you know, the numbers, we’re not talking about number of 311 calls. We’re not talking about number of calls. We’re talking about 566. And so, it just seems like a number that is very, very doable if the data is published once per year.
If I may, though?
Yeah.

And again, I’m not saying no. I’m just saying, I think, it may be a little more complicated than you’re describing, and I think one of the issues here, and the DA referred to this, it’s the five DAs, but also juvenile stuff which is not– it’s not insignificant.

That’s different. Like, that’s going to be through Corporation Counsel, and that data is going to be, again, because it’s juveniles, that is going to be more complicated. So, again, I’m not– I’m not saying no. It’s not my place to say no. I understand where you’re coming from, Council Member.

If the data were available and– is the NYPD willing to publish this data alongside the arrest, the arrest information that is already existing on the dashboard so communities can easily see and identify and digest the information?
I will certainly take it back.
Okay.
I will certainly take it back.

This looks like a real place where we can enhance reporting. We have an NYPD and a DAs office that seems very willing and able to do this. I think we have to do the work to get it done. But I’m pleased to hear that the data’s collected and that the NYPD’s willing to do it. We’ll work out the details.
I will take it back to the Police Commissioner. We will certainly explore it.
Yeah.
Just jump in for a second. Is that 566 reported or confirmed?
No, that’s confirmed. Over 2025, there were 566 total confirmed hate crimes in New York City.
And do you know how many of them were anti-semitic?
Anti-Jewish or anti-semitic, 327.
Thank you.
So, it’s 58 percent.

Director Wisdom, how are you? She has a mic. I want to talk a little bit about the office that you now head. Congratulations on this really important office that’s addressing antisemitism, the hate crime that makes up more than any other hate crime combined. And again, as I mentioned in my opening, all the other things that aren’t hate crimes, but force a

Jewish person to hide their Star of David or take off their yamika, or not participate in school and activities, your work is really important. And I’m interested to hear a little about the work that you’re going to do. So, can you talk a little bit about what stakeholders you’ve already engaged with in your listening tour and how many listening sessions you’ve done?

Sure. Thank you for the question. I agree it’s very important and I’m honored to be heading this office. So, I started this role on March 4th, so we’re really kicking into gear right now. The first group that we engage in our office was the Interagency Taskforce to Combat Antisemitism. So, that’s representatives from across agencies who’ve been deemed the appropriate person to think about that agency’s response to antisemitism and prevention. Those have been one-on-one meetings as well as a poll [sic] group meeting that will continue to engage and think through thought partnership and best practice sharing and talking to each other about trainings and what works and also learning from each other what’s happening. For example, Parks, how they deal with antisemitism is

very different than the Office of the Medical Examiner or New York City schools.
So, you’ve met once, and what’s your schedule? Is it quarterly, annually? What’s the schedule?

We’re identifying that now, what’s the best– what’s the best thing to do. I mean, each of these agencies deal with this in such different ways that it might make sense to have smaller groups that sort of have more robust antisemitism programming more frequently than those, for example, like the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner or Department of Finance who don’t. So, we’re in conversation with them about what makes the most sense right now, and happy to report that back when we have that information. We’ve also– the listening tour just kicked off last week, so we’re just getting that underway and still scheduling with stakeholders across the city. The plan is to have those in sort of small groups. I don’t think we’re– we’re sort of following the process of the Whitehouse National Strategy to combat antisemitism where they met with a thousand people from across the country, again, in sort of groups to get feedback and ask some

specific questions related to the expertise of those people and some general questions about antisemitism. So, some of those have been scheduled. Many of them are yet to be scheduled. We’re still having conversations across communities about who should be in those and making sure we’re not leaving any stone unturned. That will go on over the next couple of months, and the plan is then to release sort of a public document to– with like a focus group report, essentially, although it’s not a formal focus group. Just to talk about takeaways and what we’ve learned and what that– how that’s going to influence the programming and policy that we plan to implement over the next four years.
And when is that report due?
When is it due?
Or when is the goal for releasing that report?
We have said before the High Holy Days, so I think it depends kind of how many conversations–
[interposing] Depends on the moon?
It could be, you know, late summer I think is the goal.
Okay.
But we haven’t committed to a specific day, but obviously, you will all be the first to receive it.

Okay. You know, one of the things important to this council, but particularly me, as a former teacher, and even in some of the testimony– a quarter of antisemitic activity are against children. A quarter of the Anti-Jewish hate incidents have target children or places where children frequent, including our schools. So, what is your plan to address inside and outside the school to address a quarter of Jewish hate incidents?

So, for the six weeks that we’ve been operational, the beginning of this has really been trying to understand just as you are what this means, who this is affecting, what this looks like specifically. We are really devoted to addressing this serious problem with a scalpel and

not a sledge hammer. We want to be really thoughtful and strategic and ensure that the interventions we’re suggesting in partnership with the agencies. Like in this case New York City Public Schools or private schools around the city, and are informed by the lived experience of Jewish New Yorkers. So, I’m not prepared to say yet what we’re going to do, because we haven’t yet had enough of these conversations. But we are aware of this data as well and taking very seriously the responsibility to think about hate crimes and biases incidents affecting children wherever they gather. And we’ll again report back once we have ideas on policy and programming related to that.

And we have– let’s say– a pretty talented mayor when it comes to social media and communication. It’s pretty good. But you’re– the Mayor’s Office– the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism doesn’t, like have a website to be up?

So, we didn’t inherit a website or any social media in the previous administration, but we are in talks internally about what is the best communication channels for the admin

and certainly exploring. We want a way for the public to get in touch with the us are– so, expect that to be operational very soon do learning how to do that.

I would add do that social media. I mean, to be fair, you didn’t inherit a good social me– I mean, it may have been fine, but I think everyone understands that Mayor Mamdani’s social media was communicated with a lot of people very effectively. And so the same question about the website I have for social media which is, is your office or the mayor prepared to have social media campaigns to address– as we’ve discussed the high number of youth that are perpetrating these acts of antisemitism?

So, as per social media for our office, that’s something that’s still being explored. Again, what are other mayor’s offices doing and what are our sort of administration-wide comms practices? As for the mayor’s social media, I think that you’ve seen that he’s been both responsive to antisemitic incidents as well as talked about prevention and the importance of combatting antisemitism including, for example, last

week when he went to the Queensborough College Kupferberg Holocaust Center, and then you know, posted about that on social media and the importance of “Never again.” I imagine that he will continue to both respond to incidents and use his platform for prevention. I don’t know the specifics of his social media plans, though.
Right. I know you’ve been there for six weeks, but I would just imagine that part of your strategy is a robust social media campaign and having a website.
If we learn from–
[interposing] Is it part– is having a website and–
[interposing] Oh, having a website, yes, but again–
[interposing] A robust social media campaign, is that part of– again, given the strengths of this administration, is that part of your strategy?

Certainly using all communications channels to talk about prevention of combatting antisemitism, yes. As far

as a robust social media campaign, that has not yet been planned, but it’s certainly among the many things that we’re considering as we talk to Jewish New Yorkers and hear about what they want and need from this administration.

Yeah. I would repeat, given the number of incidents which we don’t know, but we know a large number are youth. Also, given the number of victims that are youth that need to ensure at every step of the way they see that our city is there for them or that– or potential perpetrators are learning from our city, I think it’s critical that you are using the strength of this administration leveraging those to actually– to combat antisemitism, to make that a robust part of your office. And this is a question for all of you. We touched on this with the training, but I know we wanted to move on to other questions, but I really want to kind of dig into it which is the training. And you mentioned it was part of– antisemitism training was part of the curriculum that all officers undergo, but then you said– you kind of listed all of them. Like, you know, kind of lumping antisemitism into the same legal bucket as other forms of hate.

And it is true, when they are prosecuted, you are looking at antisemitism from a legal perspective, but there’s more than the legal perspective. There’s the cultural competency that needs to exist from our patrol officers which I know you mentioned misconduct, but it is the case that patrol officers turn people away or tell them it’s not antisemitism or just say, oh, that’s political speech, it’s not– and it gets under-reported, or people feel like they can’t report to the NYPD, and they’re discouraged from reporting to the NYPD. So, I just want to be very clear, is when officers are trained on what acts of bias look like, is it general acts of bias, or is it, hey, this is how the Jewish community is experiencing antisemitism and here’s what you need to understand about it that may be unique?

Thank you very much for the question, Chair. Anecdotally, because it’s not a rote curriculum when answering your question, when we find precincts with spikes specifically of hate crimes, and obviously because of the numerical value associated with anti-Jewish incidents, we’ll speak to that. Our dedicated attorney for the Hate Crime Taskforce will go and

conduct roll call training in those precincts where we see a spike of antisemitic incidents. And as a result, that would speak anecdotally to the core competency of understanding the basis of both a bias incident and a hate crime, and what antisemitism looks like in that specific command in and around the crimes that were reported at that time.

So, it seems responsive. Like, what do you– I mean, just waiting– it’s sort of– it’s a weird order to do it in too, because what it sounds like you’re saying is it’s responsive. When you see a spike in hate crimes, you respond by going and doing some sort of training. I am interested in what that looks like as well, but if it’s going under-reported, it may not trigger the need for that training to come in.

I want to push back on that a little bit. I mean, you say responsive. I would say tailored to what’s happening in the community. I think that's actually really important, right? Hey, are things that we’re seeing. Here are things to watch for. I think that’s actually– that’s particularly effective. That’s not some abstract general thing. Here are the

possibilities. Hey, here’s what we’re seeing on the ground. Here’s what you need to watch for. I think that’s actually– that’s actually really important.

Yeah, I do– I just do want to say– I don’t think I cited this before. That in 2022, the Office of Prevention of Hate Crimes did a report on hate crimes and one of what it spoke of was under-reporting. And one of the things it said is some of the following reporting barriers were identified by respondents trying to report and not being taken seriously was one of the things that they reported. And so we have people reaching out to our offices. You have a report from New York City saying that this is an issue. And so, what is the barrier for making sure that when they get trained for the first time, they’re getting these core cultural competencies, and you’re not– and you can also be responsive, which is good. That’s what we want. We want an NYPD that’s responsive. But we don’t just want them to be responsive. We want them to be proactive. What are the barriers to ensuring the NYPD officers get this training so that they take people seriously and understand that people have to be taken seriously?

Well, I would say that what is not a barrier is the training that’s provided at the police academy. It’s provided to sergeants upon promotion, lieutenants upon promotion, and captains upon promotion. What we do is we augment those four areas that I’ve explained with what you just labeled to be reactive training at the roll call level from our Hate Crime attorney. And the question you have may not be specific to simply anti-Jewish. I could be applied to the whole universe of hate crimes, because obviously under-reporting is something that’s a conversational piece across every protected class, and so it’s imperative for our front line officers and sergeants and lieutenants and captains to understand that when any incident regardless of whether it is a bias incident, a hate crime or a police-related incident is addressed by the officer having that conversation with the complainant or victim with professionalism and a grasp of their experience.

Okay. I mean, I’m not sure– I’m not sure I quite grasp everything. And by the way, just to be clear, you know, we’re here to address antisemitism, because it is the number one

reported hate crime. Just to be clear, it’s not to the exclusion of other people’s as you’ve sort of suggested, right? Like, every people deserve to be seen and heard, and I’m– what I’d love to hear from the NYPD is just an affirmative yes, we train our officers to identify all sorts of cultural competencies so we can hear communities in which we were not raised, that we understand, and that we are not under-reporting, that we are pushing it up the ladder to make sure that at the start that it is reported.

Well, Council Member, I mean, we– this is obviously incredibly important to the Department which is why at every stage we’re training on this, right? In the academy, every time someone gets promoted, right, that reflects– we have to make choices about training, right? We can’t train on everything. The fact that we train on this time and again and again and again speaks to how important this is, how core this is for the Department. The fact that we have a taskforce that does just this shows how important it is to the Department. No matter what– and then– and then when we’re seeing spikes, the further– I would

say very like tailored follow-up, doing this at roll calls, we actually see as a whole of department focused on exactly what you’re talking about. Now, to the extent officers still fall short, that’s a problem. And I really– if there’s a complaint to your office, you should please bring that complaint to us so we can address it appropriately both to make sure that the victim is heard, and that– that underlying incident is addressed, and so that we can take appropriate disciplinary actions, because that matters, too. There’s a piece of it, right, that we’re going to train on this time and again. It’s a priority for the Department. And to the extent individual officers for whatever reason are falling short, there are consequences. That matters too. But I really want to emphasize that we do take this incredibly seriously. We do train on this, and there’s a training– again, like, really at every core opportunity that we have.

Yeah, I– the question isn’t intent. But I don’t think anyone up here is saying like, yeah, let’s have more antisemitism. The question is the actions being taken, and that’s why we’re all here, and I think

we’ve done a– you know, clarified a number of really important things, a number of next steps that can address this. I do want to turn it over to Council Member Epstein, but I think it is important for us to just know not whether or not training is being given, but what it looks like. And I think that is a clear distinction. And I’m going to turn it over to him, but I think that’s a further conversation that we need to have to make sure that we know officers are being trained in the proper meets cultural competencies before they have– you have to go in and be responsive.
